sn11.8:1.3: Verocana, “son of Virocana” is called Bali at [dn20:12.9](). His story is detailed in various legends of later times. He was a great king of the titans who at times even defeated the gods and ruled heaven, but did so justly. Here he seems to have settled his long enmity with Indra.
sn11.8:2.1: The Upaniṣad says the “highest man” (_uttamapuruṣa_) is the one who rises up from his body and manifests in his own form as the perfect light (8.12.3).
sn11.8:2.2: The Sutta substitutes _attha_ (“goal, purpose, good”) for the Upaniṣad’s _ātman_ (“Self”) in line with the dictum, “the goal is spoken of, but the self is not involved” ([an3.72:6.3](), [an6.49:4.3]()). | For _nipphadā_ (“accomplishment”), Pali has the prefixed form _abhinipphanna_ (“produced, manifested”), which appears in the same sense at [mn101:29.3]() and [sn47.10:6.11](). And that is the form the root appears in the Upaniṣad, in the sense of the Self that “achieves” or “emerges into” in its own true form (8.12.2). This is the culminating teaching of the entire Upaniṣad.
sn11.8:2.3: Pali texts read this phrase as either _nipphannasobhano attho_ (nominative singular) or _nipphannasobhino atthā_ (dative singular). I propose both phrases are found, as suits each speaker. The titan Verocana makes a banal assertion and brands it as his own wisdom. The god Sakka improves it by pointing to the cause, echoing [sn11.4:7.3](). This echoes the narrative form of Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7–12, where Virocana is easily satisfied with surface teachings, taking only the body to be the Self. | The “splendid” or “shining” (_sobhana_) goal recalls the “highest light” (_paraṃ jyotir_) of the manifest Self.
sn11.8:2.4: 8.7.1 has: _prajāpatiḥ iti ha uvāca_, Prajāpati once said
sn11.8:3.4: Indra and Virocana spent 32 years as Prajāpati’s students. Satisfied, Virocana left, while Indra stayed for a total of 101 years.
